description:
Hey! I’m working on the Lunar Landing Site Navigator challenge building a tool that helps visualize sunlight and Earth-visibility windows at candidate Artemis south pole landing sites so mission planners can quickly compare sites and dates.

I’ve been digging into the NASA datasets (LOLA terrain, JPL Horizons API) and have a solid understanding of what the challenge is asking for. I’m interested in 3D visualization, and building tools that make complex data easy to understand.
summary:
Lunar Landing Site Navigator is an interactive 3D tool, built in Unreal Engine 5, for choosing where and when to land on the Moon. It places the Sun, Earth and stars where NASA/JPL’s DE440 ephemeris puts them, for any hour from 2026 to 2030, over real terrain from NASA’s Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter.

Users pick one of 139 curated sites, or any coordinate, and scan it. The app traces the site’s true skyline in 360 directions, then forecasts a maximum of 60 days (in a single scan) of solar power, sunlit time, longest night, Earth visibility and communication blackouts. A horizon chart, a 3D sky dome and a surface view show the Sun and Earth relative to the local horizon. Users can test mast heights and a lander’s power budget, see which Deep Space Network stations can hear the site, and compare sites side by side.

This matters because power and communication decide whether a lander survives. At the south pole, where Artemis and commercial missions are headed, the Sun and Earth skim the horizon, so a single ridge can cut off power or contact. Our tool makes those trade-offs visible in minutes, and its eclipse predictions match NASA’s catalogue within three seconds.
details:
Lunar Landing Site Navigator: Project Details

A lander lives or dies by its horizon

Lunar Landing Site Navigator is a real-time 3D planning tool that answers two questions for any point on the Moon and any hour from 2026 to 2030: will this lander have sunlight for power, and can it talk directly to Earth?

On the Moon those answers are decided at the horizon. Near the south pole, where Artemis and commercial landers are headed, the Sun never climbs more than a few degrees and Earth bobs just above and below the skyline. A single ridge ten kilometres away can cut off power for days or silence a lander for two weeks.

Our app makes that visible. It places the Sun, Earth and stars where NASA's JPL ephemeris says they are, wraps them around real terrain measured by NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter, and traces the true skyline of any site in seconds. The result is a 30-day forecast of power and communication that a mission planner, a student or a judge can read at a glance, and it has been checked against NASA's own eclipse predictions to within three seconds.

What it does

In about three minutes, a user can go from the whole Moon to a side-by-side comparison of landing sites. The app is built around that journey.

1. Explore a Moon that is true to the date. Orbit and zoom a 3D Moon built from LRO terrain. Drag the timeline to any hour from 2026 to 2030 and watch the day-night line sweep across craters, Earth change phase and rotate, and the real stars turn overhead.

Screenshot 1: Moon (in shadow), sun, earth and stars positioned based on ephemeris data

Screenshot 2: Moon surface built from the LRO terrain data with the help of Cesium ion

2. Choose a site. Browse 139 curated sites in 11 categories, from Apollo landings and robotic missions to planned commercial deliveries and south-pole candidates. Each has a photo, a short description and tags. Or type any latitude and longitude.

Screenshot 3: crosshair focused on the Apollo 11 Tranquility Base with it’s description on the left

Screenshot 4: list of sites that come under the Robotics category and their locations marked on the moon as orange dots

3. Scan the horizon. One click traces the site's true skyline in 360 directions across real terrain. It takes a few seconds.

4. Read the 60-day forecast. A graph shows solar power for the next 60 days, for both Sun-tracking and flat panels. Beside it are the sunlit percentage, the longest dark period and a countdown to the next sunrise or sunset. A strip underneath shows when Earth is above the horizon, with the percentage of time in contact and the longest communication blackout.

5. See the sky from the site. A horizon chart draws the terrain skyline with the paths of the Sun and Earth over it, scaled automatically so that a polar site's few critical degrees fill the chart. A 3D sky dome shows the same paths over the site, and a surface view puts the user on the ground, with arcs at the screen edge that point to the Sun and Earth when they are out of frame.

Screenshot 5: horizon chart and the sky dome on the selected site (Apollo 17 Lunar Roving Vehicle) with the graphs showing flat panel and tracking panel power production followed by the earth visibility. Additional statistics of the scan shows in the right side of the screen

Screenshot 6: another site scan now the horizon view replacing the power generation and earth visibility graphs. Sun and earth paths are tracked in relation to the horizon in yellow and blue dotted lines

6. Engineer the mission. Raise the mast to see what a taller antenna or solar array would gain. Turn on the power budget, enter a panel area, cell type, load and battery, and the app simulates the battery through the month. It returns a verdict (viable, marginal or not viable) and the battery size the site would actually need.

Screenshot 7: power generation analytics for a scanned site based on the characteristics of the craft given by the user. The blue line (battery charge) reaches zero and therefore this specific mission is identified as Not Viable

7. Check the link. Switch to Earth view to see NASA's three Deep Space Network complexes on a correctly rotated Earth, and which of them can see the Moon at that moment.

Screenshot 8: a close-up view of the earth created using the NASA blue marble textures. The marker for Goldstone – one of the deep space network sites is visible with the angle with the moon calculated.

8. Compare. Add each scanned site to the comparison and read them side by side: sunlight, power, longest night, Earth contact and longest blackout.

Screenshot 9: the comparison view showing scan information of 4 sites one after the other for easy comparison

9. Learn it in three minutes. A built-in guided tour walks a new user through 23 steps. It highlights each control and moves on by itself when the user completes the action.

Screenshots 10–13: different steps of the tutorial. Notice Instructions given in brown UI elements and yellow outlines as hints on various elements

How it works

The app has two halves: an offline pipeline that turns NASA's flight-grade data into compact tables, and a real-time engine that combines those tables with streamed terrain to answer questions on demand.

Figure 1. From NASA data to mission answers: the offline pipeline and the real-time app.

  • Offline, in Python. NASA's SPICE toolkit computes where the Sun and Earth appear from the Moon for every hour of five years. Other scripts build the site catalogue and a star field of 41,487 real stars.
  • At run time, in Unreal Engine 5. One module turns any moment into Sun, Earth and star positions. Another scans the terrain around a site and turns the result into power and communication forecasts. The rest draw the scene and the interface.

One design decision shapes everything else: the Moon never moves. The whole scene is built in the Moon's own body-fixed frame, with the Moon fixed at the origin and the Sun, Earth and stars moving around it. That keeps the streamed terrain stationary and precise, and the Moon's monthly wobble (libration) simply appears in Earth's motion without any special handling.

A real sky: the NASA ephemeris pipeline

Every body in the scene is where NASA says it is. We use the same data and toolkit that NASA missions navigate with, not a simplified orbit model.

  • Source. JPL's DE440 planetary ephemeris and its lunar orientation solution, read through NASA's SPICE toolkit.
  • What we compute. The apparent positions of the Sun and Earth as seen from the Moon, corrected for light travel time and aberration. They are expressed in the Moon's mean-Earth frame, the same frame LRO's maps use, so sky and terrain line up by construction. We also compute Earth's pole and prime meridian, and the orientation of the celestial sphere.
  • How it reaches the engine. The result is a table of 43,825 hourly rows covering 2026 to 2030. Unreal interpolates between rows, which adds at most 0.00013° of error.

The same table drives everything on screen:

  • The Sun is a directional light plus a disc drawn at its true angular size, with limb darkening, by a custom shader that stays sharp at any zoom.
  • Earth sits at its true distance and size, with its real tilt, rotation and phase. Blue Marble imagery, clouds, night-side city lights and an atmospheric haze make it recognizable; the continents facing the Moon are the ones that really face it at that hour.
  • The stars are 41,487 real stars down to magnitude 8, each drawn as a pixel-sharp point with its catalogue colour and brightness, over NASA's Deep Star Maps Milky Way. They are oriented by the same ephemeris, so constellations are where they should be.
  • Night scenes are lit by earthshine. Its brightness is computed from Earth's phase and distance, and the camera exposure follows it, so the lunar night looks as bright as it physically would.

Screenshot 14: night sky consisting of Milky Way and 41,487 magnitude-8 stars with boosted brightness

A real horizon: the skyline scan

Knowing where the Sun is means little until you know what stands in front of it. The scan measures exactly that: the height of the terrain skyline in every compass direction, as seen from the lander.

Figure 2. The skyline scan: 360 directions, each searched to 0.004°.

  • Terrain. Cesium Moon Terrain streams NASA's LRO laser-altimeter (LOLA) elevation data: about 59 m resolution at mid-latitudes, sharpening to 5 m within 2.5° of the poles.
  • The search. For each of 360 directions, the app finds the skyline by binary search. It fires a 500 km ray, checks whether it hits terrain, and halves the angle range 14 times. That pins the skyline to 0.004°, using about 5,000 rays per scan.
  • Why 500 km is enough. For terrain farther away to show above the horizon, both the lander and the distant peak would need to stand 18 km above all the ground between them. Nothing on the Moon does.
  • Mast heights. The scan repeats from several heights above the ground, so the user can switch mast height and see the result instantly.

Streamed terrain created the hardest engineering problem. A streaming engine only loads fine detail near the camera, but the user is usually watching from orbit. Our solution is a second, invisible camera placed at the landing site. It forces full-detail terrain to load in every direction around the site, and the scan waits until loading is complete before it fires a single ray.

From geometry to power and communication

With the sky and the skyline in hand, the app steps through the next 30 days hour by hour (721 samples) and asks the same questions at each step.

Figure 3. How a partly hidden Sun becomes a power figure.

Solar power

  • How much of the Sun is visible? At the poles the Sun often sits half behind a ridge, so "lit or unlit" is the wrong question. The app treats the Sun as a disc of its true size (about 0.53° across) and computes the exact fraction above the skyline.
  • How strong is the sunlight? It starts from the solar constant measured by NASA's SORCE mission, 1361 W/m², and scales it by the Sun's actual distance that day, a swing of about ±4% over the year.
  • How is the panel pointed? Power is given both for a Sun-tracking panel and for a flat, upward-facing one, which collects far less at the poles where the Sun is low.
  • Is Earth in the way? During a lunar eclipse, Earth covers the Sun as seen from the Moon. The app computes the overlap of the two discs and cuts the power accordingly.

Communication

  • Is Earth above the skyline? The same disc calculation is applied to Earth, which is almost four times wider than the Sun in the lunar sky, with a 1° safety margin for a reliable link.
  • Who is listening? NASA's three Deep Space Network complexes rotate with the Earth model. A station counts as available when the Moon is at least 10° above its horizon.

What comes out

  • Statistics: sunlit percentage, average power, longest dark period, Earth-contact percentage, longest blackout, and the share of time with both power and contact.
  • Events: the next sunrise, sunset, Earth-rise and Earth-set, found by an hourly search refined 12 times to sub-second precision.
  • Power budget: the user's panel, load and battery are run through the month hour by hour. The app tracks the battery's charge, finds the deepest discharge, and reports both a verdict and the battery capacity the site really requires.

Why the south pole is the hard case

The same 30 days look completely different at the equator and at the pole, and that difference is why a horizon-aware tool is needed.

Figure 4. Sun and Earth over 30 days from 14 November 2026, on a perfectly smooth Moon: Apollo 11 against the Shackleton connecting ridge.

Screenshot 15: horizon generated by a scan based on the LRO terrain in comparison to the smooth terrain in the graph. Notice the Sun and earth going above and below this horizon line

  • At Apollo 11, the Sun climbs to 88° and then sets for two weeks. Earth hangs 59° to 73° up and never sets. Terrain hardly matters, because nothing important happens near the horizon.
  • At the connecting ridge near the south pole, the Sun circles the horizon all month, only 1° to 2° above a smooth skyline. Earth swings between 7° below and 6° above it. Everything important happens within a few degrees of the horizon.

At the pole, a hill a fraction of a degree high decides whether a lander has power or contact. The numbers in Figure 4 assume a smooth Moon; the app replaces that assumption with the measured skyline of the actual site.

Accuracy and validation

A planning tool is only useful if its numbers can be trusted, so we measured ours. Every figure below is reproducible with a script we provide.

Checked against NASA's eclipse catalogue. A lunar eclipse on Earth is a solar eclipse on the Moon: Earth passes in front of the Sun. That makes NASA's eclipse predictions an independent test of our whole sky pipeline. For all 12 lunar eclipses from 2026 to 2030, the moment our data puts Earth closest to the Sun matches NASA's "greatest eclipse" within 0.1 to 2.7 seconds. The app also agrees with NASA on whether the Sun is fully hidden, partly hidden or untouched in all 12 cases.

Figure 5. Eclipse timing: our pipeline against NASA's catalogue for every lunar eclipse from 2026 to 2030.

Screenshot 16: the date is set to 2027/08/17 – which is an eclipse date as evident from the above graph. Notice the dip in power generation at the beginning of the graph and both Sun and Earth overlapping in a sky

Screenshot 17: the horizon view set to the same date. Note the overlapping sun and earth paths above the horizon and their overlapping vectors in the sky dome

Checked against independent software. We recomputed 180 dates with Skyfield, a separate astronomy library with its own code for the ephemeris, light-time, aberration and lunar orientation. Sun and Earth directions agree within 0.0006 arcseconds, and Earth's distance within 4 metres.

An honest error budget. We traced every source of error from NASA's data to the final number and ranked them. The sky is not the limit: the largest uncertainty is how much terrain detail is loaded during a scan.

Figure 6. Error budget: every source of angular error on one scale.

We also state what the tool cannot promise. At polar sites the Sun slides sideways along the skyline, so exact sunrise and sunset times are sensitive to small terrain errors, while monthly percentages are robust. The app's coordinate table labels every site by how its position was obtained.

What makes it different

Excellent lunar tools already exist, and we built on the same NASA data they use. What did not exist, as far as we could find, is a single tool that turns that data into a mission answer: power in watts, contact in hours, a battery verdict, and a side-by-side choice between sites.

Existing tool

What it is good at

What it leaves to the user

NASA Moon Trek

A map portal with many data layers and analysis tools, including slope, lighting and Sun-angle calculation

It is a general mapping portal. Turning Sun angles into power, blackout and battery figures for a mission is left to the user

LROC QuickMap

An expert map browser with 3D shadows, Sun and Earth positions and a visibility analysis over time

Built for specialists working with map layers. It does not produce a power budget, mast study or site-against-site comparison

JPL Horizons

Authoritative positions of any body from any location, as tables of numbers

No terrain and no picture: it cannot say when a ridge blocks the Sun

Published polar illumination maps

Average sunlight over a year across a whole region

An average cannot answer "what happens at my site in my landing month, with my mast?"

NASA SVS visualisations

Beautiful, accurate pre-rendered views of lunar lighting

Fixed films: the viewer cannot pick a site, a date or a design

Our combination is what sets the app apart:

  • It answers in engineering units. Not just lit or dark, but watts per square metre, hours of blackout, and whether a specific lander survives.
  • It handles the Sun and Earth together. Power and communication are forecast side by side for the same site and the same month, because a mission needs both.
  • It respects the partial cases. A Sun half behind a ridge, a taller mast, an eclipse: the cases that matter most at the poles are modelled, not rounded away.
  • It compares. Sites are scanned in seconds and set side by side, so the trade-off between power and contact is visible at once.
  • It is for everyone. A curated site list, a guided tour and a game-engine interface replace the map-layer expertise that existing tools assume.
  • It shows its working. Every number comes with a measured precision and a script that reproduces it.

Benefits and intended impact

The app shortens the path from "where could we land?" to "here is why this site works" from days of specialist analysis to minutes of exploration.

Who benefits

  • Mission and payload teams. In early studies, a team can screen candidate sites and landing dates, size a battery and judge whether a mast is worth its mass, before committing specialist time to detailed analysis.
  • Small teams and newcomers. University groups, start-ups and emerging space programmes rarely have a lighting-analysis specialist. The app gives them the same NASA data in a form they can use on day one.
  • Educators and students. Scrubbing through a lunar month makes libration, the two-week night and the low polar Sun visible in a way no diagram can.
  • The public. Anyone can stand at Tranquility Base or on the rim of Shackleton crater on a chosen date and see the Earth where it would really be.

What changes

  • Faster trade-offs. Power against contact, one ridge against the next, a 2 m mast against a 10 m one: each is a few clicks.
  • Fewer surprises. Partial sunlight, eclipses and communication blackouts appear in the forecast instead of after landing.
  • Shared understanding. Engineers, scientists and decision-makers can look at the same scene and the same numbers.

The intended impact is to make landing-site reasoning accessible well beyond the few groups that can do it today.

How it is creative

We treated a game engine as a scientific instrument, and borrowed ideas from games, architecture and astronomy to make orbital geometry readable.

  • A game engine doing mission analysis. Unreal Engine's ray casting, built for gameplay, measures the lunar skyline. Its real-time lighting shows the answer the moment a date changes.
  • A universe that moves around the Moon. Fixing the Moon and moving everything else is the reverse of how the scene is usually imagined, and it removed whole classes of precision and streaming problems.
  • Pointers borrowed from games. In surface view, arcs at the screen edge point to the Sun and Earth when they are out of frame, the way action games point to an off-screen threat.
  • A sun-path dome borrowed from architecture. Architects draw the Sun's path over a building as a dome. We draw the Sun's and Earth's paths over the landing site the same way, in 3D, resized to stay readable from orbit.
  • A horizon chart that adapts to the site. It stretches itself so that a polar site's few critical degrees fill the panel, and it states the stretch factor so the picture stays honest.
  • A sky built from catalogues. Each of 41,487 stars is a real catalogue entry drawn as a sharp point, not a blurred photograph wrapped on a sphere.
  • A physically lit night. Earthshine brightness comes from Earth's phase, so the lunar night is dim at new Earth and silver-bright at full Earth, as it would be.

What we considered

  • Accuracy against speed. Running NASA's toolkit inside the engine was possible but heavy. A precomputed hourly table costs 0.0001° of accuracy and makes time scrubbing instant.
  • One frame for everything. The sky uses the same lunar reference frame as LRO's terrain, so the two cannot drift apart.
  • Honesty about limits. We measured our errors, published them, and tell users which outputs are robust (monthly percentages) and which are sensitive (exact polar sunrise times).
  • Everyday users first. Specialist features such as the power budget are switched off until wanted, so the default screen stays simple.
  • Trust in the site list. Each site records how its coordinates were obtained, from positions measured in LRO images to approximate published figures.
  • Responsible use of data. Every dataset and image is credited with its source and licence.
  • It has to run elsewhere. The app is a packaged build that streams terrain on demand, so the download stays small.

Tools, languages, software and hardware

The app is built in Unreal Engine 5 with Blueprint visual scripting, fed by Python scripts that prepare and validate NASA data.

Area

What we used

What it does in the project

Engine

Unreal Engine 5.8.4

Real-time rendering, ray casting for the skyline scan, packaging for several environments

App logic

Blueprint visual scripting

All simulation and analysis logic.

Interface

Unreal Motion Graphics (UMG)

Timeline, site browser, compare window and tutorial. The power graph and horizon chart are drawn directly in code

Shaders

Unreal material editor with custom HLSL

Anti-aliased Sun disc with limb darkening, pixel-sharp stars, constant-width sky-path lines, Earth's atmosphere and city lights

Terrain

Cesium for Unreal 2.31 and Cesium ion

Streams Cesium Moon Terrain, built from NASA LOLA data, with a lunar georeference

Data preparation

Python 3 with SpiceyPy (NASA's SPICE toolkit) and NumPy

Builds the 5-year hourly ephemeris table, the site catalogue and the star-field mesh

Validation

Python 3 with Skyfield, pyerfa (IAU SOFA) and SciPy

Independent recomputation, Earth-orientation check, eclipse timing against NASA

Formats

CSV data tables, binary glTF, EXR, JPEG

The star field is written as a glTF mesh by our own script

Build tools

Visual Studio 2022

Compiling and packaging

3D and texturing

Blender for modeling and texturing the earth alongside NASA Blue Marble textures

Provides a realistic-looking Earth and gives realistic bounce lighting for the dark side of the moon

NASA data used: the JPL DE440 ephemeris and lunar orientation through SPICE, LRO laser-altimeter terrain, landing coordinates measured in LRO images, Blue Marble Earth imagery, Deep Star Maps 2020 and Deep Space Network station locations. The full list is in the NASA Data section of this submission.

Limits and next steps

The app is a screening tool for early decisions, and we know where its edges are.

Current limits

  • Terrain detail. Results depend on how much detail is streamed during a scan. Boulders and small craters beside the lander are below the terrain data's resolution.
  • Internet required. Terrain is streamed, so the app cannot scan offline.
  • A 60-day window. Forecasts cover one month at a time from the chosen date.

Next steps

  • Relay satellites. Add lunar relay orbits such as NASA's Lunar Communications Relay and Navigation Systems (LCRNS) so that far-side and polar blackouts can be closed.
  • Seasonal and yearly statistics. Extend the forecast to a full year to capture polar summer and winter.
  • Rover traverses. Scan along a route to plan drives that stay in sunlight and in contact.
  • Exportable reports. Save a site's forecast and comparison as a document or data file.
  • Offline terrain. Cache the terrain for chosen regions so the tool works without a connection.
  • Thermal environment. Use the same Sun geometry to estimate surface and hardware temperatures.
